chapters.title: How Translations Change Meaning — and Why the Bible Leaves Out Its Culture
chapters.subtitle: From Hebrew and Greek to your Bible: what is gained, what is lost, and why
chapters.nutshell: The Bible was written for people who already shared its culture, so it rarely explains customs. Then it travelled through many languages: Hebrew and Greek, then Latin, then English and Tamil. At each step translators had to make choices, and some words slowly took on new shades of meaning.
chapters.bigIdea: Every translation is an honest attempt to carry meaning across a gap of language and culture, and knowing the gaps helps you hear the original voice.
skeleton: The Bible speaks to insiders who already know the culture
Sometimes writers stop and explain customs for outsiders
The text travels: Hebrew → Greek → Latin → English
Translators choose between word-for-word and thought-for-thought
Some key words shifted meaning along the way — for understandable reasons
Using several translations and the original words gives a fuller picture

p: The Bible was first written for people who lived inside its world. They knew how a wedding worked, what a Samaritan was and why hands were washed before meals. Writers did not need to explain these things, just as a letter to your family does not explain your family's habits. Scholars call this “high-context” communication: much of the meaning sits in shared background, not in the words.

Yet sometimes the writers do stop to explain. Mark tells his non-Jewish readers how Pharisees wash hands, cups and pots (Mark 7:3–4). John explains that the stone jars at Cana were “for the Jewish rites of purification” (John 2:6) and that “Jews have no dealings with Samaritans” (John 4:9). These little notes show that the Gospels were already reaching outsiders.

sections.h: The long journey of the text
p: The Old Testament was written mostly in Hebrew (with some Aramaic). From the 3rd century BC Jews in Egypt translated it into Greek; this is the Septuagint. The New Testament was written in Greek and often quoted that Greek Old Testament. Later the Western church used Latin, and Jerome's Vulgate (about AD 405) became its Bible for a thousand years.

The first complete English Bibles (Wycliffe, 1380s) were translated from the Latin. Tyndale (1526 onward) went back to the Greek and Hebrew. Words that had been shaped by Latin church use, however, often stayed in English Bibles, and many of them passed into other languages too.

No two languages match exactly. Translators must decide how closely to follow the original wording. A “formal” (word-for-word) translation keeps the shape of the original, even when it sounds stiff. A “dynamic” (thought-for-thought) translation rewrites the meaning in natural modern speech. A paraphrase goes further still.

Each approach has strengths. Word-for-word versions let you see repeated words and images; thought-for-thought versions are easier to understand at first reading. Reading two kinds side by side is one of the simplest ways to notice where the original says something richer than one English or Tamil word can hold.

Some changes came through Latin. Greek *metanoia* means a change of mind and direction (like Hebrew *teshuvah*, “return”). Latin *paenitentia* could also mean regret or penalty, and medieval readers linked it to the church practice of penance. Tyndale rendered *ekklēsia* (“assembly”) as “congregation”, but later Bibles kept “church”, a word that had come to mean a building and an institution.

Other changes come from merging words. The KJV uses “hell” for Hebrew *Sheol* and Greek *Hades* (the grave or realm of the dead), *Gehenna* (the valley of Hinnom used as a picture of judgment) and *Tartarus* (2 Pet 2:4). These are different ideas in the original. Modern versions often keep the original names so readers can see the difference.

sections.h: Names, titles and a famous debate
p: The Hebrew name Ya'akov became Greek Iakōbos and Latin Iacobus. In English the Old Testament form became “Jacob”, but later forms of the Latin name gave us “James” for the New Testament men. The brothers of Jesus and the apostles carried the patriarch's name (the Tamil Bible keeps யாக்கோபு for both). In Isaiah 14:12 the Hebrew means “shining one, son of the dawn”; Latin *lucifer* (“light-bringer”, the morning star) passed into the KJV and later became a name for Satan in Christian tradition.

God's personal name YHWH was not spoken aloud by Jews out of reverence; readers said *Adonai* (“my Lord”). The Septuagint used *kyrios* (“Lord”), and English Bibles print “LORD” in capitals. In Isaiah 7:14 the Hebrew *almah* means a young woman of marriageable age; the Septuagint chose *parthenos*, usually “virgin”, and Matthew 1:23 quotes it. Jewish readers stress the Hebrew word; Christians read the verse in the light of Jesus' birth. Both sides are reading real words honestly.

chapters.title: The Septuagint and the Story of Bible Translations
chapters.subtitle: From Alexandria to Tranquebar: how the Bible reached every language
chapters.nutshell: The Septuagint is the Greek translation of the Hebrew Scriptures, made by Jews in Egypt before Jesus' time. The New Testament writers and the early church often used it. Alongside it stand the Hebrew Masoretic Text, the Dead Sea Scrolls and many later translations, right down to the Tamil Bible.
chapters.bigIdea: God's word has always been translated so that ordinary people can hear it in their own language.
skeleton: A legend of 72 elders, and what history actually shows
Why Greek-speaking Jews needed a Greek Bible
The New Testament and early church use the Septuagint
Hebrew copies: Masoretic Text and Dead Sea Scrolls
Latin, English and Tamil translations follow

p: The Letter of Aristeas tells a famous story. King Ptolemy II of Egypt wanted the Jewish Law for his great library in Alexandria, so 72 elders, six from each tribe, came from Jerusalem and translated it in 72 days. The name Septuagint (“seventy”, written LXX) comes from this story.

Historians think the story is idealised, but its core fits the evidence: the Torah was translated into Greek in Alexandria in the 3rd century BC. The other books followed over the next generations, mostly by about 100 BC. Different translators worked in different styles, some very literal, some free.

After Alexander the Great, Greek became the common language of the eastern Mediterranean. Many Jews, especially in Egypt, spoke Greek better than Hebrew. They needed the Scriptures in the language they used every day, both in the synagogue and at home.

When the apostles wrote, the Septuagint was the Bible of most Greek-speaking Jews. The New Testament writers often quote it, sometimes where it differs from the Hebrew. The early church used it as its Old Testament. Partly because Christians used it, Jews later made new, more literal Greek versions: Aquila (about AD 130), Symmachus and Theodotion.

sections.h: The Hebrew text: Masoretes and Dead Sea Scrolls
p: The Hebrew Bible most translations use today is the Masoretic Text. The Masoretes were Jewish scholars (7th–10th centuries AD) who added vowel signs, accents and careful notes to protect every letter. Its best complete copies are the Aleppo Codex (about AD 930) and the Leningrad Codex (AD 1008).

In 1947 the Dead Sea Scrolls were found near Qumran. The Great Isaiah Scroll is about 1,000 years older than the Leningrad Codex, yet it agrees with it to a remarkable degree, with mostly small differences. Some scrolls agree with the Septuagint against the Masoretic Text, showing that the Septuagint sometimes translated a different Hebrew copy.

The Samaritans kept their own Hebrew Torah, the Samaritan Pentateuch. Jews in Aramaic-speaking lands used Targums, Aramaic translations that often explain as they translate. Syriac-speaking Christians used the Peshitta. The earliest Latin versions (the Old Latin) were made from the Septuagint.

Around AD 382–405 Jerome made a fresh Latin translation. For most of the Old Testament he went back to the Hebrew, which he called the “Hebrew truth” (*Hebraica veritas*). His Vulgate became the Bible of the Western church.

sections.h: From the Reformation to the Tamil Bible
p: Wycliffe's followers translated the Vulgate into English in the 1380s. After printing and Erasmus' Greek New Testament (1516), Tyndale translated from Greek (1526) and Luther gave Germans their Bible (New Testament 1522, whole Bible 1534). The King James Version followed in 1611; later came the RV (1881), RSV (1952), NASB (1971), NIV (1978) and ESV (2001), using older manuscripts found in the meantime.

In 1714 Bartholomäus Ziegenbalg, a German missionary at Tranquebar, published the Tamil New Testament, usually called the first Bible translation printed in an Indian language. Later revisions by Fabricius (18th century) and Rhenius (19th century) led to the Tamil Union Version (around the 1860s–1870s), still widely used through the Bible Society of India.
